title: The First Three Minutes

sources.where: Choudhuri Ch. 10.7 (T = 1.52e10/√t K, eq. 10.67; T in MeV = 1.31/√t, 10.69; |Ω−1| ∝ t, 10.70), 11.1-11.2 (relativistic gases 11.9-11.19), 11.3 (BBN, n/p 11.20-11.23), 11.4 (neutrino background), 11.5 (dark matter), 11.6 (inflation), 11.7 (recombination, last scattering), 11.9 (structure formation)
HS25 winter: open Q7 (radiation era, BBN)

intro: Run the film backwards: the Universe gets hotter as $T\propto1/a$. At 1 s it is a $10^{10}$ K soup of photons, electrons, positrons and neutrinos with a pinch of neutrons and protons; at 3 minutes helium forms; at 380 000 years atoms form and the CMB is released. Each step is set by one comparison: a reaction rate against the expansion rate $H$.

encounters.title: The cosmic clock: temperature versus time

blocks.html: In the radiation era $a\propto t^{1/2}$ and $T\propto1/a$, so $T\propto t^{-1/2}$. Putting in the constants (photons only, Choudhuri (10.66)-(10.69)):

Timeline (energy ↔ time): $\sim10^{-35}$ s inflation (?); $10^{-6}$ s, 1 GeV: quarks bind into protons and neutrons; 1 s, 1 MeV: neutrinos decouple, n/p freezes, then $e^\pm$ annihilate; 3 min, 0.1 MeV: nucleosynthesis (D, He, Li); 50 000 yr, ~1 eV: matter–radiation equality; 380 000 yr, 0.3 eV ($z\approx1100$): recombination, CMB released; then dark ages, first stars at $z\sim20$, reionisation, galaxies.

A process "freezes out" when its rate $\Gamma$ drops below the expansion rate $H$: particles can no longer find each other before the Universe has doubled in size. Almost every relic (neutrinos, the n/p ratio, the light elements, the CMB) is a snapshot taken at its own $\Gamma=H$.

Energy scales the MC asks for: BBN at ~1 MeV (binding energies of nuclei; HS25 practice MC7) and recombination at ~1 eV (just below 13.6 eV because photons vastly outnumber baryons; HS24 summer MC15).

encounters.title: Photons per baryon: the number that runs cosmology

blocks.label: (11.9), (11.17)-(11.19). Both scale as a^{-3}, so η is constant after e± annihilation.

blocks.html: For relativistic particles $\rho c^2=g\frac{a_B}{2}T^4$ (bosons) or $\frac78g\frac{a_B}{2}T^4$ (fermions), with $g$ the number of spin states (photons: 2). Non-relativistic species are exponentially suppressed, $n\propto(mT)^{3/2}e^{-mc^2/k_BT}$.

There are about $1.6\times10^9$ photons for every proton or neutron. This tiny $\eta$ is why atoms and nuclei form "late": even when $k_BT$ is far below a binding energy, the high-energy tail of so many photons can still break every bound state. It is also the parameter BBN measures (through deuterium).

encounters.title: Big Bang nucleosynthesis: why a quarter of the baryons are helium

blocks.html: While weak reactions ($n+\nu\leftrightarrow p+e^-$, $n+e^+\leftrightarrow p+\bar\nu$) are fast, neutrons and protons are in equilibrium: Boltzmann with $\Delta mc^2=1.29$ MeV. The rate falls as $\Gamma/H\approx(T/0.8\,\mathrm{MeV})^3$ (11.20), so the ratio freezes at $k_BT\approx0.8$ MeV:

blocks.label: (11.21)-(11.23). Free neutron decay (τ ≈ 880 s) until fusion starts at ~3 min lowers this to n/p ≈ 1/7 and Y ≈ 0.25.

blocks.html: Fusion must wait for deuterium ($B=2.2$ MeV) to survive photo-dissociation, which happens only at $k_BT\approx0.07$ MeV ($T\approx10^9$ K, $t\approx3$ min; HS25 winter Q7 gives 225 s), again because of the $10^9$ photons per baryon (the "deuterium bottleneck"). Then nearly all neutrons end up in $^4$He.

Helium is ~25 % of baryonic mass everywhere we look, even in the oldest, most metal-poor gas: it cannot have been made in stars (they made only a few % since). Deuterium is fragile and only destroyed by stars, and its leftover abundance falls steeply with $\eta$: a cosmic baryometer. It gives $\Omega_b\approx0.05$, far below $\Omega_M\approx0.3$: most dark matter is not baryonic.
Each He nucleus contains 2 neutrons, so $Y=2n_n/(n_n+n_p)$ (mass fraction), not $n_n/(n_n+n_p)$.

blocks.html: Neutrinos decouple at ~1 MeV, slightly before electrons and positrons annihilate. The annihilation heats the photons (entropy of $e^\pm$ goes to photons only), so today the neutrinos are colder:

blocks.label: Three neutrino species; the factor 1.68 enters the time of matter–radiation equality.

blocks.html: There are ~340 relic neutrinos per cm³ around you, never directly detected. Massive neutrinos are hot dark matter: they move too fast to let small structures form, so they can be at most a small fraction of the dark matter.

encounters.title: Recombination and the cosmic microwave background

source.where: Choudhuri §10.5 (CMB spectrum), §11.7 (formation of atoms, last scattering surface)

blocks.html: Above ~3000 K hydrogen is ionised and free electrons Thomson-scatter photons constantly (mean free path tiny; recall Choudhuri ex. 2.7: ionised air is opaque within 14 m). At $T\approx3000$ K ($z\approx1100$, $t\approx380\,000$ yr) electrons and protons combine, the electron density drops, and photons stream freely: the last scattering surface. We see it today as the CMB, redshifted to 2.725 K.

blocks.label: A nearly perfect blackbody (COBE/FIRAS); the tiny anisotropies are the seeds of all structure.

blocks.html: The spectrum stays a blackbody after decoupling: free streaming in an expanding universe just redshifts every photon by the same factor, which maps a Planck spectrum at $T$ onto a Planck spectrum at $T/(1+z)$. That is why $T\propto1/a$ exactly.

Recombination is not at $k_BT=13.6$ eV (that would be 160 000 K). Because $n_\gamma/n_B\sim10^9$, there are still enough photons above 13.6 eV in the Wien tail until $k_BT\approx0.3$ eV. Same logic as the Saha equation for stellar atmospheres.

options: electrons and protons combined into neutral hydrogen

encounters.title: Dark matter, inflation and the growth of structure

source.where: Choudhuri §11.5 (dark matter), §11.6 (inflation, horizon and flatness problems), §11.9 (structure formation); §10.7 eq. (10.70)

blocks.html: Dark matter: evidence from rotation curves, cluster virial masses, X-ray gas, lensing, and the CMB. BBN says only $\Omega_b\approx0.05$, so most of $\Omega_M\approx0.3$ is non-baryonic. It must be "cold" (slow) to let small structures form first: weakly interacting massive particles, axions... still unknown.

Structure growth: in the matter era, overdensities on scales above the Jeans length grow as $\delta\propto a$ (a power law, not exponential, because expansion fights gravity). Baryonic fluctuations of $10^{-5}$ at $z=1100$ would have grown only to $10^{-2}$ today: not enough for galaxies. Dark matter, which does not feel radiation pressure, started growing earlier (from $z_{eq}$), and baryons fell into its potential wells after recombination.

Inflation (Guth 1981): a brief early phase of exponential expansion. It solves the horizon problem (CMB regions on opposite sides of the sky have the same $T$ to $10^{-5}$ but were never in causal contact without inflation) and the flatness problem ($|\Omega-1|\propto t$ in the radiation era and $\propto t^{2/3}$ in the matter era, so a nearly flat universe today needs extreme fine tuning early on), and its quantum fluctuations seed the $10^{-5}$ perturbations.

Flatness is unstable like a pencil balanced on its tip: any deviation from $\Omega=1$ grows. That the Universe is still nearly flat after 13.8 Gyr means it started incredibly close to $\Omega=1$; inflation drives it there naturally by making $a$ huge, $|\Omega-1|\propto1/(aH)^2$.

encounters.title: Helium mass fraction from the frozen n/p ratio
encounters.goal: Show that $Y=\frac{2(n_n/n_p)}{1+n_n/n_p}$ if all neutrons end up in $^4$He, and evaluate it for $n_n/n_p=e^{-1.29/0.8}$ and for $1/7$.

steps.reveal: Each He-4 holds 2 n + 2 p. With $n_n$ neutrons, helium contains $2n_n$ nucleons; total nucleons $n_n+n_p$. $Y=\frac{2n_n}{n_n+n_p}=\frac{2(n_n/n_p)}{1+n_n/n_p}$.

encounters.goal: Flat, radiation only, $\rho\propto a^{-4}$, $\rho\propto T^4$. Show $a\propto t^{1/2}$, $T\propto t^{-1/2}$, and find $t_{BBN}$ for $T_{BBN}=10^9$ K given $T(1\,\mathrm s)=1.5\times10^{10}$ K.

encounters.title: Counting the CMB photons
encounters.problem: $n_\gamma=\frac{2\zeta(3)}{\pi^2}\left(\frac{k_BT}{\hbar c}\right)^3$ with $\zeta(3)=1.202$, $T_0=2.725$ K, $\hbar=1.0546\times10^{-34}$ J s. Baryons: $\Omega_bh^2=0.0224$, $\rho_{c}=1.879\times10^{-26}h^2$ kg m$^{-3}$.

steps.hint: $k_BT/\hbar c\approx1190$ m$^{-1}$. About 410 photons per cm³.
Choudhuri (11.18): $11.3\,\Omega_bh^2$ m$^{-3}$, a quarter of a proton per m³.
